** `momentum_health` was entirely absent from this bundle — no status, no MTUM/SPMO drawdown figures, no signals block — despite CLAUDE.md naming it as a required input to the regime step on *every* run, and this was precisely the week its answer mattered most. I had to infer the factor unwind by hand from `sector_relative_strength` (every AI-stack sector strongly positive on 3m and sharply negative on 1m while SPY was flat), which is a slower and less auditable read than the tool that already exists. Worse, the failure is silent: the fail-open convention treats a missing block as "unknown, no adjustment," which is indistinguishable in the pack from a genuine `unknown` verdict on live data — so on a `weekly_market` depth the gather can drop the block entirely and nothing surfaces it. The fix is small: have the gatherer emit `momentum_health` on every depth (weekly included) and, when it genuinely cannot compute, emit an explicit `{"status": "unavailable", "reason": ...}` stub so the pack distinguishes "the factor is fine" from "nobody looked."

** `momentum_health` came back **null** this run — the factor-unwind detector produced no reading in precisely the week it mattered most, with hyperscaler enablers −34.3%, design IP −20.6% and servers −18.7% over one month while SPY held flat. That is the textbook momentum-unwind signature the module exists to catch, and its silence means the validator's automatic risk-budget halving would *not* have fired had this been a trading depth. It should fail *loud* (log the reason and surface `status: unavailable` in the bundle) rather than fail silently to null. Secondary: `market_radar` gainers and losers came back as four all-null rows — expected on a Sunday with no session, but they should be omitted or labeled `no_session_data` rather than served as empty objects that look like a populated sweep. That module exists specifically to catch this pattern and to halve new-BUY risk budgets via `momentum_unwind_risk_scale`, and it was silent during the clearest example the book has seen. Both losses shared the same demand_driver (hyperscaler_server_capex/servers_hardware) dressed up as two separate theses when the actual catalyst language ('SMCI collapse consolidates AI-server share') was nearly identical -- bad reasoning (thin diversification), not bad data, and it is exactly the clustering the system's theme-risk cap now exists to prevent. HPE's exit was graded process_fail: I closed it at $46.08 without its $43.75 stop being hit and without a clearly named invalidator firing -- conviction cracked, not thesis broken, which is the discretionary-exit mistake I need to stop making. What I got right: after those two losses on 7/15, the book stayed disciplined and all-cash through the rest of the week, including declining a real-looking AMD dip-buy today because my own stated trigger condition (post-event confirmation) was not actually met. The one change for next week: before any discretionary SELL_TO_CLOSE that isn't a stop or horizon exit, I will name the specific thesis_invalidator that actually fired in the sell thesis itself -- if none of the three stated invalidators fired, the move is to hold or trim with sell_fraction, not a full discretionary close.

** The deterministic trigger check fired on AMD purely because the *price* touched the parsed $500 level, but my published `would_buy_at` was a compound condition — *post-event* confirmation plus a 50-DMA reclaim, explicitly excluding a pre-event dip. The result is a full event-driven run spun up for a setup that was never actually live, five days before its own catalyst. The trigger parser could be materially sharper if it also parsed an *event/date gate* from the trigger text (e.g. "after 7/22-23") and suppressed or down-weighted the alert until that date passes, rather than firing on the price alone. That would save event-driven runs for triggers whose *conditions*, not just prices, are met — reducing exactly this kind of "premature trigger" cycle.

** The single highest-value fix this run is upstream of my judgment: the orchestrator handed me a portfolio reading `$0 equity / $0 cash / no positions` with no `data_quality` or `stale_data_notice` flag raised, even though the trade history mathematically implies ~$982 should exist. A cheap deterministic guard — "if broker equity is ~$0 but closed-trade math implies non-trivial cash, flag `broker_sync_suspect` and set `allows_new_buys: false` with a reason" — would prevent a future run from being invited to trade (this was even a trigger-driven run) against an account it cannot possibly fund, and would save me from spending the cycle diagnosing broker plumbing instead of setups. Separately, the watchlist trigger checker should parse the *qualitative* half of `would_buy_at` (here, "confirmed positive reaction to the 7/22-23 event... not a bounce off today's low") rather than only the first dollar figure, so it stops firing event-driven runs on price alone before the event has occurred.

** Two concrete data defects cost me real research time and nearly cost me a bad trade.

`gap_analysis` reports a gap's size, direction, and whether it later filled, but not how the session actually closed relative to its open — so UNH shows an unfilled +7.4% gap while `pct_change_1d` is only +1.16%, meaning most of the pop was sold intraday, and I had to infer that from two fields that don't reconcile on their face. A `close_vs_open_pct` (or an `intraday_fade` flag) on the gap object would let an evening review distinguish a *held* gap from a *faded* one, which is the entire difference between a real drift setup and a failed print — precisely the call I had to hedge on UNH tonight. Secondary: `momentum_health` was absent from this bundle entirely (not even `unknown`), and `position_histories` was `skipped`, so two documented inputs to the regime read were silently missing rather than explicitly null.

Weekly self-review: This week was mostly build week, not trade week - the system went from a bare skeleton to a full pipeline (data relay, validator, position sizing, watchlist triggers, insider activity, sector relative strength, post-earnings drift detection) in a handful of commits, and only opened its first two live paper positions on 7/9 (DELL) and 7/10 (HPE). Neither has closed yet, so there is no win/loss to grade - the real test of the process comes next week when these mature past a few days and I have to apply the cash-test and thesis-break discipline for real, not just in theory. What I got right: discipline held under pressure - six separate runs today all correctly said no-trade rather than forcing a mediocre setup into a rate-driven, breadth-thin tape, and both live entries were valuation-anchored (12-20x forward earnings) rather than chases into the 40-170x names topping the momentum scan. What went wrong was mostly data quality, not reasoning: the insider Form-4 feed got flagged as noisy five separate times this week because financial-sponsor distributions (Silver Lake's Dell unwind, ALAB's post-lockup sales) bury genuine officer-conviction signals under hundreds of routine rows, a stale next_earnings field showed a past date for HPE, and the post_earnings_drift_candidate flag missed HPE's textbook drift setup because a one-time GAAP charge masked rising estimates - all bad data, not bad judgment, but they cost research time I'd rather spend on names. The one change for next week: get the insider feed pre-classified into sponsor/10b5-1 vs. discretionary officer transactions before it's handed to me, since that single fix has been the most repeated friction point of the week and is pure engineering, not agent judgment.

** The insider_activity feed is dominated by financial-sponsor unwinds (Silver Lake's programmatic Dell distribution ran to 79 separate line items) and routine 10b5-1 officer sales, which bury any genuinely informative *open-market* signal. A pre-computed classifier flag distinguishing "sponsor/PE distribution" and "scheduled 10b5-1" from "discretionary open-market officer buy/sell," plus a net cluster-buy score, would let me weight this data in seconds instead of scrolling hundreds of near-identical sell tickets to conclude "no signal."

** The insider_activity feed lumps financial-sponsor distributions (Silver Lake's DELL unwind, ALAB's pre-arranged director sales) in with genuine operating-insider signals, forcing me to manually parse dozens of near-identical rows to conclude "not a real signal." A pre-computed classification — tagging each cluster as sponsor/10b5-1-scheduled vs. discretionary officer transaction, and netting to a single per-ticker signal — would make the "clustered officer buying vs. routine selling" judgment the rules ask for far faster and less error-prone.

** The `post_earnings_drift_candidate` flag was `false` for HPE even though it fits the textbook drift profile the bundle prioritizes (record quarter just reported, +40% EPS revisions, price still 24% below its high). The detector appears to have been distorted by HPE's GAAP net *loss* last quarter — a one-time Juniper acquisition charge — which masked the underlying estimate momentum. Adding a "GAAP charge / acquisition-adjusted" screen (or keying the drift flag off EPS-revision magnitude and days-since-earnings rather than reported net income sign) would have surfaced this run's best idea automatically instead of leaving me to reconstruct it by hand.

** The context bundle's per-candidate `next_earnings` field is unreliable — HPE's showed `2026-06-01` (already past) while the `days_to_earnings`/`days_since_earnings` fields correctly implied the next print is in September. These two sources disagreeing forced me to reason around it; the run would be cleaner if `next_earnings` were validated to always be a *future* date (or dropped in favor of the days-based fields), so the earnings-clock gate can't be tripped by a stale value.

** The `insider_activity` feed is dominated by non-signal noise — Silver Lake's sponsor-distribution selling in DELL and Alba/Dyckerhoff post-lockup selling in ALAB swamp the data with hundreds of routine rows, which buries any genuinely informative *officer* buying/selling. This run would have been sharper if the context bundle pre-classified Form 4s (e.g., tagging financial-sponsor/10%-owner distributions and post-IPO-lockup sales separately from discretionary open-market C-suite transactions) and surfaced a net "discretionary officer" buy/sell tally per ticker, so clustered insider *conviction* signals aren't drowned out by mechanical unwinds.

** The context bundle gives me valuation and price/momentum but no consensus estimates or forward revenue-growth figures, so I'm forced to lean on trailing fundamentals plus headline sentiment when judging whether a rich multiple (ANET at 41x, ALAB at 97x) is justified. Adding forward revenue-growth and EPS-revision (analyst estimate trend) fields per candidate would materially sharpen the "is this multiple deserved" call and reduce reliance on qualitative news vibes — the single biggest lever on proposal quality this run.

** The context bundle deep-researches only the top-5 by deterministic score, but two of those five (TXN, AMD) are effectively un-actionable this run because of earnings timing (7/22) or a same-day news gap — meaning I burned my richest data (filings, 13F, news) on names I won't trade, while candidates like HPE and CRDO that I'm actively weighing had only a price and momentum row. Adding a `next_earnings` field and a `days_to_earnings` flag directly into the `universe_scan.top_setups` rows (not just the news block), plus expanding SEC/news enrichment to the top 8 rather than top 5, would let me screen out earnings-binary setups before spending research budget and give me fundamentals on the names I actually end up considering.
